prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Do not use dashes, semicolons, colons or parentheses.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
Everything below happens before the browser receives the first byte of the response, and most of it takes only a few hundred milliseconds. Take an address like https://www.example.com/shop as the running example. The browser works through several stages in order.

**Parsing the address**

The browser first splits the address into parts. The scheme is https, the host is www.example.com, the port is implied as 443 because that is the default for https, and the path is /shop. The browser checks whether the host is on its HSTS list, which is a record of sites that must only be reached securely. It also checks for a service worker or a cached response that could answer the request without touching the network. If a fresh cached copy exists, the process ends here and no bytes cross the network at all.

**Finding the server with DNS**

Networks route traffic using IP addresses, not names, so the browser must translate www.example.com into an address. It looks in its own DNS cache first, then asks the operating system, which checks its own cache and a local hosts file. If neither knows the answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver. This is usually run by your internet provider or a public service, and it does the hard work on the browser's behalf.

If the resolver has no cached answer, it asks a root server which servers handle the com zone. It then asks a com server which servers handle example.com, and finally it asks that domain's authoritative name server for the address of www.example.com. Every answer carries a time to live value that tells resolvers how long they may cache it. Because of this caching, most lookups finish in a few milliseconds. A cold lookup can take noticeably longer, and it is one reason the first visit to a site often feels slower than later ones.

The answer may contain both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Browsers typically try both and use whichever connects first. Modern browsers may also learn from a special HTTPS DNS record that the server supports HTTP/3, which affects the next step.

**Opening a connection**

With an IP address in hand, the browser needs a channel to the server. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 this is a TCP connection, established by a three step exchange called the handshake. The browser sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN and ACK, and the browser answers with an ACK. That costs one full round trip, which is the time for a message to reach the server and a reply to return. If the server is far away, a round trip might be 100 milliseconds or more, so every extra round trip is felt directly.

HTTP/3 works differently. It runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP and folds the connection setup and the encryption setup into one exchange. If the browser knows or guesses that the server supports HTTP/3, it may skip the separate TCP stage altogether. Browsers often race the two approaches and keep whichever wins.

Before any of this, the browser may reuse an existing connection to the same host. Connection reuse is a major optimisation, because it removes both the handshake and the encryption setup from the cost of a request.

**Securing the connection with TLS**

Because the address uses https, the connection must be encrypted and the server must prove its identity. This is the job of Transport Layer Security, or TLS. In TLS 1.3 the browser sends a ClientHello message that lists the encryption methods it supports and includes its half of a key exchange. It also includes the server name it wants, using an extension called SNI. This lets one IP address host many sites and still present the right certificate.

The server replies with its own half of the key exchange and its certificate. Both sides can now calculate the same shared secret without ever sending it across the network. The server also sends a signature that proves it holds the private key matching the certificate. From this point on, everything is encrypted.

The browser then validates the certificate. It checks that the certificate covers www.example.com, that the dates are valid, and that it chains up to a certificate authority the browser or operating system already trusts. It may also check that the certificate has not been revoked. If any check fails, the browser shows a warning page and does not send the request.

TLS 1.3 needs one round trip. Older TLS 1.2 needs two. If the browser has talked to the server before, it can resume the session using a saved ticket and may even send data immediately, a feature called early data.

**Sending the request**

The secure channel is now ready, and the browser finally sends the HTTP request. In HTTP/1.1 this is plain text that looks like a request line saying GET /shop HTTP/1.1, followed by headers. The Host header names the site, the Accept header says which content types the browser can handle, and the Accept-Encoding header offers compression such as gzip or Brotli. The User-Agent header identifies the browser. Any cookies that belong to this site and path are attached as a Cookie header. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry the same information in a compact binary form and compress the headers, but the meaning is identical.

**What the server does**

The request travels across the network, often arriving first at a CDN or load balancer rather than the origin server. A CDN edge server may already hold a cached copy and respond immediately. Otherwise the request is forwarded to the origin, where a web server hands it to application code. That code might check a session cookie, query a database, render a template, and build a response. Slow database queries and heavy rendering show up here as waiting time.

**The first byte arrives**

Once the server has something to send, it writes the status line and headers, such as 200 OK and a Content-Type header, followed by the start of the body. The moment the first byte of that response reaches the browser, the stage described here ends. Developers measure this interval as Time to First Byte, or TTFB.

Seen as a whole, TTFB is the sum of the DNS lookup, the connection setup, the TLS handshake, the request travelling to the server, the server's processing time, and the first byte travelling back. When a page feels slow to start, checking each part in the browser's network panel tells you which part to fix.
